title: Master Class | GM's Blunder Too, Vienna Gambit | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: e4, e5 — an open game. We've been leaning on the Danish Gambit lately, but let's switch it up.
A knight to c3 — the Vienna. It's a phenomenal opening for anyone below master strength, largely because Black players simply don't study this move.
And a bishop to c5 is already a little inaccurate — the very reaction the Vienna preys on.
The whole idea of the Vienna Gambit is to improve on the King's Gambit: develop the knight first, watch how Black sets up, and only then play f4 — so you're better placed to meet a capture on f4.
And it turns out the bishop on c5 does nothing to stop f4, which a lot of people don't realize.
So f4 anyway. The bishop on c5 doesn't prevent it.
Black takes on f4. This is the hot-button moment, because we have to reckon with a queen check on h4.
A knight to f3 is essential — you can't answer a queen check on h4 with g3 because the f4 pawn just captures it. The knight to f3 covers h4 and is the best move here.
Black plays d6, holding the center — and we still have to keep an eye on that queen check.
And here I play a knight to d4 — a genuine blunder that simply drops the knight. Damage-control time.

Black captures on d4 and we've backed ourselves into a corner — down a knight, with the queen check on h4 still looming. We can't meet g3 with a recapture because both our rook and the pawn would hang.
A queen to f3 begins the recovery: now, if the queen comes to h4 and we answer g3 and the pawns trade, both the rook and the pawn are defended.
Black captures on c3 to trade — but that's already a small win for us, because that bishop was a monster. When you're down a piece, the priority is development.
We recapture with the d-pawn on c3 — the fastest route to quick development. We'll castle long, since the kingside is already wrecked.
Black plays g5 to defend the f4 pawn — another subtle mistake, because we're castling queenside and if his king goes short he'll pay dearly for that advanced pawn.
A bishop to d2, prioritizing development and king safety so we can start attacking. It isn't pretty, but we need to castle as fast as possible.

Castling long is the fastest way to safety. I don't care in the slightest about the a2 pawn — if Black grabs it we play b3 and trap the bishop; when you're down a piece you can't fret over a single pawn.
Black plays a6. Now, the idea I taught last game: when there's a pawn chain, attacking its base can make the whole structure topple.
So h4 — striking the foot of Black's g5-f4 chain. Knock out the base and the whole thing collapses.
We take on g5 to make that foot collapse. I know Black wants a bishop to g4, pinning my queen to the rook, but we're ready to give the exchange to topple his kingside.
Black plays the bishop to g4, and we'll sacrifice another exchange to make his whole kingside cave in.
The queen captures on f4 — we have to preserve the queen while Black grabs the rook.
Black takes our rook, landing on d1, and now we choose what to capture — because something very cool happens here.

After we recapture on f6, Black's bishop is trapped: it retreats to h5, but we've opened the h-file and our rook covers that square. That's the kind of thing that just falls into your lap when you play aggressively and hunt for chances.
Black plays a bishop to c2 — this still isn't better for White if he defends correctly, and he isn't defending badly.
The king recaptures on c2. He's given the bishop for a pawn.

Now we act on our strong f6 pawn — a great anchor for our pieces. The question is what Black wants: he won't castle kingside, since we'd mate him at once, so he'll try to castle queenside via a queen to d7, and we must stop that. A bishop to g4 tempts, but it has a drawback.

So g3 first, preparing a bishop to h3 instead — the difference being that after a bishop to e2 and g4, Black's knight to e5 covers g4; routed through h3, the bishop is far better protected. Same number of moves, better result.
Black plays a knight to e5.
And we go to h3 with the bishop.

Black's knight comes to g6 — but he still can't get his queen out; his pieces are stuck in molasses. He hits our queen, so we move it to a square that keeps the f6 pawn defended — that pawn is a huge bargaining chip.

A queen to f5. Not a queen to e3, which drops the pawn; not to f3, where a knight back to e5 hits it again; and not to g5, where h6 harasses it. f5 also builds a battery — a queen to d7 could be mate.
Black plays c6. We want to open the center, because he's paralyzed and any opening favors us. Here's the thought experiment: if you could remove one of your own pawns, which would it be?
The e-pawn, of course — so paradoxically, rather than a slow rook move first, just play e5 to clear it and free the e-file for the rook.
Black replaces the pawn by capturing on e5. You can sacrifice your rook for his pawn, but never for your own — you have to make him be the one to take it.
A rook to e1, and now we're threatening to capture on e5 with a mating attack.
Black finds a defense with a queen to c7 — so we pile onto the knight, keeping our eyes on the target.
A bishop to f4, adding an attacker to the knight so we can blast through with a capture on e5.
The king steps to d8.
We take on e5 with the bishop.
Black recaptures on e5.
And now a rook to d1 with check, so the rook can swing into d7.
The rook lands on d7, attacking the queen — it has to move, and the rook will swing to e7.
Black plays a queen to a5.
We begin with a check on e7, forcing the king toward f8 — if it goes to d8 instead, a queen to d7 is mate.
The king goes to f8. Now we just win it normally.
We need to attack f7 while posing as many threats as possible — the queen does that far better from h5 than from d7.
Black tries a queen to d5.

The reason h5 is better: from there the queen also has a check on h6 and a mate on g7. When you have an idea while attacking, develop and sharpen it — this is a forced mate, so we pre-move the queen to g7.
He resigns. A very instructive game.
The move f4 is often misunderstood.
People think it's impossible because of a bishop capture on g1 — after we recapture with the rook, a queen check on h4 sends chills down your spine.
It looks terrible — we block the check and Black grabs a pawn. But take the bigger view: Black has developed exactly one piece, the queen, the very piece you don't want out this early.
As long as White handles the immediate threats, White is completely winning — that queen is essentially stranded.
You can't trap it right away, and you don't even want the pawn — you want to blast open the center.
So d4, seizing the window while Black is undeveloped and the queen is in Timbuktu — the engine reads about plus six.
After the trade on d4 White is completely winning — castle quickly, threaten to trap the queen, and it's crushing, because Black simply hasn't developed and the center is already open.
So the bishop capture on g1 is nowhere near as good as it looks.
The capture on f4 is also an error — Black should play d6, keeping the central pawn chain alive.
After the capture and a knight to f3, you see why the bishop on c5 is misplaced: d4 comes with tempo.
d4 gives White a phenomenal position.
After the bishop retreats, a capture on f4 leaves White with the center and great development — a queen to d2, castle long, and enjoy your life; castling short is fine too.
Here you can even castle short — nothing wrong with it at all.
I did play that genius knight blunder, of course — I revealed Fabi's high-level novelty, so I'll have to give him a call.
After the knight to d4, the capture, and the queen to f3, our opponent played very well but began a series of subtle mistakes.
What should Black have done? Simplest is to prioritize development — a queen check on h4 to start, then g3.
After the trades and a queen to g4, that bishop is Black's best piece, monopolizing the whole center — so capturing on c3 was wrong, it gave us air and sped up our development.
Most importantly it accelerated the development of our king.
If Black had checked on h4 before we took the knight, we'd answer g3.
And a bishop to g2, and we're still very much in the game — though the other way was totally winning too.

Recapturing on d4 isn't bad; after the trades and g5 we again prioritize queenside development and king safety. That g5 was a big waste of time — a knight to f6 or c6 was better. When you're up a piece, trading is not the priority: play exactly as you would with equal material. That's my single most important piece of advice — the closer you play to a level-material game, the less you'll go wrong, and the same is true in the endgame.
